Title: Comparative Study on Surgical Trainees’ Performance in Laparoscopic Surgery: Origami Box Folding Exercise vs. Outside-the-Box Knot Tying Exercise

Overview and Background
Surgical trainees’ psychomotor skills in minimally invasive surgery benefit from simulation exercises that target spatial visualization, hand–eye–tool coordination, fine motor control, and knot-tying precision. Two commonly used dry-box exercises are the origami box folding exercise (OBFE), which emphasizes free-hand folding of a target shape within a laparoscopic box, and the outside-the-box knot tying exercise (OTBKT), where trainees tie standardized knots with limited workspace and potentially dominant-hand movement out of the box. <cite id="803587f7-1">This study directly compared OBFE and OTBKT across surgical residents, reporting measurable changes in time, errors, and self-assessment</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Independent work has shown origami-based training improves Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) scores, suggesting transfer to broader psychomotor domains</cite>.

Task Definitions and Measurement Approaches
- Origami box folding (OBFE): Trainees fold an origami target (e.g., crane or box) using two forceps inside a restricted dry-box workspace, emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, spatial planning, and precision. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami crane training required completing a 7.5×7.5 cm crane under a laparoscopic dry box, with quality scored on a 15-point scale and demonstrated to enhance hand–eye and bimanual coordination</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">A resident-based origami “LOT” curriculum shortened time to complete cranes and was associated with significantly reduced time to establish pneumoperitoneum in real cases</cite>.
- Outside-the-box knot tying (OTBKT): Trainees perform extracorporeal and/or intracorporeal knots on a box trainer, often with the dominant hand partially outside the box, under timed and error-based scoring (e.g., OSATS procedural subdomains, knot quality, and defined technical error categories). <cite id="f38b9769-0">Knot tying instruction and assessment on a box trainer used error-free instructional videos, adapted OSATS for knot tying, a 5-point knot quality rubric, and a 2-minute time limit for proficiency, aligning with experienced surgeon performance levels</cite>.
- Metrics: Objective measures include task completion time (surgical and square knots), out-of-visual-field instrument excursions, needle drops, tissue lesions, and technical error counts; subjective measures include Likert-scale self-assessment of knowledge/technique. <cite id="803587f7-1">A prospective cohort applied BOB-based software to quantify performance and paired nonparametric tests for within- and between-group comparisons</cite>.

Comparative Findings: OBFE vs. OTBKT
In a prospective cohort of 84 residents (34 OBFE, 50 OTBKT) across general surgery, obstetrics–gynecology, and urology, both methods significantly improved surgical knot-tying performance, with similar absolute reductions in surgical-knot time (OBFE −316.65 s; OTBKE −360 s; p = 0.96 for between-group difference) and comparable error-rate improvements. <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE showed a larger improvement for square knots (−278 s vs. −169 s for OTBKE; p = 0.02), indicating differential learning effects by knot type</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-1">Technical error reductions improved in both groups and self-rated surgical-knot knowledge improved more in OBFE (p = 003), with larger effect sizes for self-assessment in OBFE (0.84–0.87) vs. OTBKE (0.77–0.85)</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-4">These conclusions reiterate that both OBFE and OTBKE effectively improve laparoscopic skills, with OBFE favoring square-knot efficiency and self-rated knowledge gains, whereas OTBKE is more targeted to surgical-knot mechanics</cite>.

Learning Patterns and Error Profiles
- Time-based learning: <cite id="803587f7-1">Surgical-knot time improved substantially in both groups over the intervention, with OBFE achieving slightly greater absolute reductions</cite>. <cite id="81669725-1">Across FLS tasks including extracorporeal and intracorporeal knot tying, simulator box training reduced completion time over 12 months for multiple tasks (with extracorporeal and intracorporeal knots improving), although loop ligation time did not improve</cite>. <cite id="81669725-2">Precision cutting and peg transfer showed time reductions, yet passing rates depended on baseline proficiency, illustrating ceiling effects</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">In OTBKT-specific settings, proficiency criteria combined time (≤2 min), OSATS procedural score (≥11/13), and knot quality checks (gaps, tight base, opposed edges, stability), aligning with expert performance benchmarks</cite>.
- Error reduction: <cite id="803587f7-1">Both OBFE and OTBKE reduced technical errors similarly, suggesting each modality addresses general psychomotor slip-ups (e.g., out-of-field instruments, needle drops, tissue lesions)</cite>. <cite id="81669725-3">Error-based scoring on simulators accumulates penalty points per error type, providing granular feedback that can be tracked over training cycles</cite>.
- Self-assessment and perceived knowledge: <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE produced greater gains in self-rated knowledge of surgical knots and had larger effect sizes in Likert assessments, potentially reflecting enhanced spatial and bimanual conceptualization from origami-based practice</cite>.

Transfer to Broader Competencies and Clinical Performance
- FLS and psychomotor generalization: <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Prospective data show that 4-week origami crane training under a dry box significantly increased Total FLS score (164 ± 48 pre to 1107 ± 112 post) and brought subtask levels (peg transfer, loop ligation, extracorporeal ligation) toward proficiency, consistent with enhanced hand–eye and bimanual coordination</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Methodologically, this single-arm study used weekly FLS assessments and a 15-point crane quality rubric, while acknowledging limits such as small sample size and unknown clinical transfer</cite>.
- Clinical outcomes: <cite id="803587f7-3">A longitudinal, controlled comparison of residents trained with laparoscopic origami “LOT” versus untrained residents showed significantly shorter pneumoperitoneum setup times (129 vs. 208.5 min; p < 0.001), supporting transfer of simulator-derived coordination to operating-room efficiency</cite>.
- Simulator-task cross-generalization: <cite id="81669725-0">Residents undergoing FLS simulator box training exhibited decreased time for multiple tasks (peg transfer, precision cutting, extracorporeal and intracorporeal knots), with extracorporeal knot time decreasing over 6–12 months, though passing rates depended on task and baseline</cite>. <cite id="81669725-1">These findings suggest that structured simulator sessions can improve both time-based metrics and confidence, with residents endorsing improved surgical skills and patient safety</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Task-specific proficiency criteria on box trainers (time, OSATS procedural, knot quality) provide an objective bridge between simulator learning and expert-level performance expectations</cite>.

Practical Implications: When to Use Which and Sequencing
- OBFE strengths: <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE improved square-knot efficiency more than OTBKE and enhanced self-rated knowledge, indicating utility for foundational spatial and bimanual coordination and conceptual understanding of geometric transformations</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami-based dry-box practice improves FLS composite and subtask performance, suggesting broad psychomotor transfer</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">Programmatic integration of origami training correlates with faster intraoperative setup, supporting efficiency gains in the OR</cite>.
- OTBKT strengths: <cite id="803587f7-1">OTBKE produced comparable improvements in surgical-knot time and reduced technical errors overall, with targeted refinement of surgical-knot mechanics under tight workspace constraints</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Use of structured checklists (OSATS procedural, knot quality, time limits) ensures that trainees internalize precision, tension management, and error avoidance typical of minimally invasive knot tying</cite>.
- Recommended sequencing: <cite id="803587f7-1">Evidence supports using OBFE to build foundational spatial and bimanual skills and knowledge, followed by OTBKE for targeted, high-fidelity practice in surgical knot tying that generalizes to constrained box environments</cite>.

Limitations and Considerations
- Population and task specificity: <cite id="803587f7-1">The direct OBFE vs. OTBKE comparison enrolled residents across three surgical specialties, which enhances generalizability but may mask within-specialty differences</cite>. <cite id="81669725-2">Certain tasks (e.g., loop ligation) may require more practice or show smaller time improvements, highlighting that not all FLS subtasks benefit equally from the same training dose</cite>.
- Measurement fidelity: <cite id="803587f7-1">Performance quantification combined instrument excursion, needle drops, tissue lesions, and self-assessment; reliance on simulator-based metrics and Likert scales can limit ecological validity</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Prospective origami-to-FLS studies were single-arm with small samples and acknowledged selection bias and unknown clinical outcome effects, underscoring the need for larger randomized trials with hard endpoints</cite>.

Summary and Recommendations
- Head-to-head evidence shows both OBFE and OTBKE improve laparoscopic knot-tying performance, with similar overall time reductions and error-rate improvements; OBFE confers greater square-knot efficiency gains and larger self-rated knowledge improvements, whereas OTBKE offers focused surgical-knot refinement under constrained workspace. <cite id="803587f7-1">These differences support a staged curriculum: early OBFE to develop spatial and bimanual coordination and conceptual knowledge, followed by OTBKE for high-fidelity, task-specific knot tying</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-4">Both exercises are effective and can be implemented sequentially to broaden psychomotor skill sets and knowledge retention</cite>.
- Beyond direct comparisons, origami-based dry-box practice correlates with higher FLS scores and faster intraoperative setup, indicating transfer to broader psychomotor competence and OR efficiency. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami crane training markedly improved Total FLS scores and subtask proficiency levels</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">Residents with prior origami training achieved significantly shorter pneumoperitoneum times</cite>.
- Implementation guidance: Pair OTBKE with OSATS-procedure and knot-quality checklists and time limits to calibrate to expert benchmarks; integrate OBFE early with iterative quality rubrics for folding precision to build spatial and bimanual foundations; monitor self-assessed knowledge to capture cognitive transfer. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Use adapted OSATS and knot-quality rubrics and enforce realistic time thresholds for proficiency</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-1">Track instrument excursions, needle drops, tissue lesions, and time for both tasks, and leverage larger self-assessment effect sizes as a proxy for durable conceptual gains</cite>.

Evidence Gaps and Future Directions
- Randomized controlled trials directly comparing OBFE-first vs. OTBKE-first sequences with intermediate FLS and hard OR outcomes would clarify optimal sequencing and transfer. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Existing single-arm origami-to-FLS studies call for larger, prospective cohorts and clinical outcome studies</cite>.
- Cross-task standardization is promising but needs expansion: harmonized metrics spanning box folding, knot tying, and peg transfer could quantify g-factor transfer and identify subgroups benefiting differentially from each modality. <cite id="81669725-1">Task-specific time and pass-rate deltas across 12 months suggest variable learning curves, motivating tailored curricula</cite>.

Key Takeaways for Trainees and Educators
- Use OBFE early to strengthen spatial visualization, bimanual coordination, and knot-knowledge foundations; expect larger gains in self-rated knowledge and square-knot efficiency. <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE improved square-knot time more than OTBKE and increased self-rated knowledge</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami training significantly elevates FLS scores and approaches proficiency on multiple subtasks</cite>.
- Reserve OTBKE for targeted practice under constrained workspace; expect comparable surgical-knot time improvements and robust error reduction, with the added benefit of high-fidelity checklist-based mastery. <cite id="803587f7-1">OTBKE reduced surgical-knot time by ~360 s and lowered technical errors</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Proficiency criteria combining time, OSATS procedural, and knot quality approximate expert performance</cite>.
- Integrate both to enhance learner readiness: evidence supports a sequence—origami box folding first, then outside-the-box knot tying—to comprehensively build and refine laparoscopic psychomotor competence. <cite id="803587f7-1">Both methods are effective; OBFE may precede OTBKE to optimize foundational skills and targeted refinement</cite>.

Conclusions: Both OBFE and OBTKE effectively improve laparoscopic skills in surgical residents. OBFE is particularly beneficial for square knot efficiency and self-rated knowledge enhancement, while OBTKE focuses on targeted knot-tying training. Title: Comparative Study on Surgical Trainees’ Performance in Laparoscopic Surgery: Origami Box Folding Exercise vs. Outside-the-Box Knot Tying Exercise

Overview and Background
Surgical trainees’ psychomotor skills in minimally invasive surgery benefit from simulation exercises that target spatial visualization, hand–eye–tool coordination, fine motor control, and knot-tying precision. Two commonly used dry-box exercises are the origami box folding exercise (OBFE), which emphasizes free-hand folding of a target shape within a laparoscopic box, and the outside-the-box knot tying exercise (OTBKT), where trainees tie standardized knots with limited workspace and potentially dominant-hand movement out of the box. <cite id="803587f7-1">This study directly compared OBFE and OTBKT across surgical residents, reporting measurable changes in time, errors, and self-assessment</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Independent work has shown origami-based training improves Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) scores, suggesting transfer to broader psychomotor domains</cite>.

Task Definitions and Measurement Approaches
- Origami box folding (OBFE): Trainees fold an origami target (e.g., crane or box) using two forceps inside a restricted dry-box workspace, emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, spatial planning, and precision. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami crane training required completing a 7.5×7.5 cm crane under a laparoscopic dry box, with quality scored on a 15-point scale and demonstrated to enhance hand–eye and bimanual coordination</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">A resident-based origami “LOT” curriculum shortened time to complete cranes and was associated with significantly reduced time to establish pneumoperitoneum in real cases</cite>.
- Outside-the-box knot tying (OTBKT): Trainees perform extracorporeal and/or intracorporeal knots on a box trainer, often with the dominant hand partially outside the box, under timed and error-based scoring (e.g., OSATS procedural subdomains, knot quality, and defined technical error categories). <cite id="f38b9769-0">Knot tying instruction and assessment on a box trainer used error-free instructional videos, adapted OSATS for knot tying, a 5-point knot quality rubric, and a 2-minute time limit for proficiency, aligning with experienced surgeon performance levels</cite>.
- Metrics: Objective measures include task completion time (surgical and square knots), out-of-visual-field instrument excursions, needle drops, tissue lesions, and technical error counts; subjective measures include Likert-scale self-assessment of knowledge/technique. <cite id="803587f7-1">A prospective cohort applied BOB-based software to quantify performance and paired nonparametric tests for within- and between-group comparisons</cite>.

Comparative Findings: OBFE vs. OTBKT
In a prospective cohort of 84 residents (34 OBFE, 50 OTBKT) across general surgery, obstetrics–gynecology, and urology, both methods significantly improved surgical knot-tying performance, with similar absolute reductions in surgical-knot time (OBFE −316.65 s; OTBKE −360 s; p = 0.96 for between-group difference) and comparable error-rate improvements. <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE showed a larger improvement for square knots (−278 s vs. −169 s for OTBKE; p = 0.02), indicating differential learning effects by knot type</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-1">Technical error reductions improved in both groups and self-rated surgical-knot knowledge improved more in OBFE (p = 003), with larger effect sizes for self-assessment in OBFE (0.84–0.87) vs. OTBKE (0.77–0.85)</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-4">These conclusions reiterate that both OBFE and OTBKE effectively improve laparoscopic skills, with OBFE favoring square-knot efficiency and self-rated knowledge gains, whereas OTBKE is more targeted to surgical-knot mechanics</cite>.

Learning Patterns and Error Profiles
- Time-based learning: <cite id="803587f7-1">Surgical-knot time improved substantially in both groups over the intervention, with OBFE achieving slightly greater absolute reductions</cite>. <cite id="81669725-1">Across FLS tasks including extracorporeal and intracorporeal knot tying, simulator box training reduced completion time over 12 months for multiple tasks (with extracorporeal and intracorporeal knots improving), although loop ligation time did not improve</cite>. <cite id="81669725-2">Precision cutting and peg transfer showed time reductions, yet passing rates depended on baseline proficiency, illustrating ceiling effects</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">In OTBKT-specific settings, proficiency criteria combined time (≤2 min), OSATS procedural score (≥11/13), and knot quality checks (gaps, tight base, opposed edges, stability), aligning with expert performance benchmarks</cite>.
- Error reduction: <cite id="803587f7-1">Both OBFE and OTBKE reduced technical errors similarly, suggesting each modality addresses general psychomotor slip-ups (e.g., out-of-field instruments, needle drops, tissue lesions)</cite>. <cite id="81669725-3">Error-based scoring on simulators accumulates penalty points per error type, providing granular feedback that can be tracked over training cycles</cite>.
- Self-assessment and perceived knowledge: <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE produced greater gains in self-rated knowledge of surgical knots and had larger effect sizes in Likert assessments, potentially reflecting enhanced spatial and bimanual conceptualization from origami-based practice</cite>.

Transfer to Broader Competencies and Clinical Performance
- FLS and psychomotor generalization: <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Prospective data show that 4-week origami crane training under a dry box significantly increased Total FLS score (164 ± 48 pre to 1107 ± 112 post) and brought subtask levels (peg transfer, loop ligation, extracorporeal ligation) toward proficiency, consistent with enhanced hand–eye and bimanual coordination</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Methodologically, this single-arm study used weekly FLS assessments and a 15-point crane quality rubric, while acknowledging limits such as small sample size and unknown clinical transfer</cite>.
- Clinical outcomes: <cite id="803587f7-3">A longitudinal, controlled comparison of residents trained with laparoscopic origami “LOT” versus untrained residents showed significantly shorter pneumoperitoneum setup times (129 vs. 208.5 min; p < 0.001), supporting transfer of simulator-derived coordination to operating-room efficiency</cite>.
- Simulator-task cross-generalization: <cite id="81669725-0">Residents undergoing FLS simulator box training exhibited decreased time for multiple tasks (peg transfer, precision cutting, extracorporeal and intracorporeal knots), with extracorporeal knot time decreasing over 6–12 months, though passing rates depended on task and baseline</cite>. <cite id="81669725-1">These findings suggest that structured simulator sessions can improve both time-based metrics and confidence, with residents endorsing improved surgical skills and patient safety</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Task-specific proficiency criteria on box trainers (time, OSATS procedural, knot quality) provide an objective bridge between simulator learning and expert-level performance expectations</cite>.

Practical Implications: When to Use Which and Sequencing
- OBFE strengths: <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE improved square-knot efficiency more than OTBKE and enhanced self-rated knowledge, indicating utility for foundational spatial and bimanual coordination and conceptual understanding of geometric transformations</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami-based dry-box practice improves FLS composite and subtask performance, suggesting broad psychomotor transfer</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">Programmatic integration of origami training correlates with faster intraoperative setup, supporting efficiency gains in the OR</cite>.
- OTBKT strengths: <cite id="803587f7-1">OTBKE produced comparable improvements in surgical-knot time and reduced technical errors overall, with targeted refinement of surgical-knot mechanics under tight workspace constraints</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Use of structured checklists (OSATS procedural, knot quality, time limits) ensures that trainees internalize precision, tension management, and error avoidance typical of minimally invasive knot tying</cite>.
- Recommended sequencing: <cite id="803587f7-1">Evidence supports using OBFE to build foundational spatial and bimanual skills and knowledge, followed by OTBKE for targeted, high-fidelity practice in surgical knot tying that generalizes to constrained box environments</cite>.

Limitations and Considerations
- Population and task specificity: <cite id="803587f7-1">The direct OBFE vs. OTBKE comparison enrolled residents across three surgical specialties, which enhances generalizability but may mask within-specialty differences</cite>. <cite id="81669725-2">Certain tasks (e.g., loop ligation) may require more practice or show smaller time improvements, highlighting that not all FLS subtasks benefit equally from the same training dose</cite>.
- Measurement fidelity: <cite id="803587f7-1">Performance quantification combined instrument excursion, needle drops, tissue lesions, and self-assessment; reliance on simulator-based metrics and Likert scales can limit ecological validity</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Prospective origami-to-FLS studies were single-arm with small samples and acknowledged selection bias and unknown clinical outcome effects, underscoring the need for larger randomized trials with hard endpoints</cite>.

Summary and Recommendations
- Head-to-head evidence shows both OBFE and OTBKE improve laparoscopic knot-tying performance, with similar overall time reductions and error-rate improvements; OBFE confers greater square-knot efficiency gains and larger self-rated knowledge improvements, whereas OTBKE offers focused surgical-knot refinement under constrained workspace. <cite id="803587f7-1">These differences support a staged curriculum: early OBFE to develop spatial and bimanual coordination and conceptual knowledge, followed by OTBKE for high-fidelity, task-specific knot tying</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-4">Both exercises are effective and can be implemented sequentially to broaden psychomotor skill sets and knowledge retention</cite>.
- Beyond direct comparisons, origami-based dry-box practice correlates with higher FLS scores and faster intraoperative setup, indicating transfer to broader psychomotor competence and OR efficiency. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami crane training markedly improved Total FLS scores and subtask proficiency levels</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-3">Residents with prior origami training achieved significantly shorter pneumoperitoneum times</cite>.
- Implementation guidance: Pair OTBKE with OSATS-procedure and knot-quality checklists and time limits to calibrate to expert benchmarks; integrate OBFE early with iterative quality rubrics for folding precision to build spatial and bimanual foundations; monitor self-assessed knowledge to capture cognitive transfer. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Use adapted OSATS and knot-quality rubrics and enforce realistic time thresholds for proficiency</cite>. <cite id="803587f7-1">Track instrument excursions, needle drops, tissue lesions, and time for both tasks, and leverage larger self-assessment effect sizes as a proxy for durable conceptual gains</cite>.

Evidence Gaps and Future Directions
- Randomized controlled trials directly comparing OBFE-first vs. OTBKE-first sequences with intermediate FLS and hard OR outcomes would clarify optimal sequencing and transfer. <cite id="a3df4bea-0">Existing single-arm origami-to-FLS studies call for larger, prospective cohorts and clinical outcome studies</cite>.
- Cross-task standardization is promising but needs expansion: harmonized metrics spanning box folding, knot tying, and peg transfer could quantify g-factor transfer and identify subgroups benefiting differentially from each modality. <cite id="81669725-1">Task-specific time and pass-rate deltas across 12 months suggest variable learning curves, motivating tailored curricula</cite>.

Key Takeaways for Trainees and Educators
- Use OBFE early to strengthen spatial visualization, bimanual coordination, and knot-knowledge foundations; expect larger gains in self-rated knowledge and square-knot efficiency. <cite id="803587f7-1">OBFE improved square-knot time more than OTBKE and increased self-rated knowledge</cite>. <cite id="a3df4bea-1">Origami training significantly elevates FLS scores and approaches proficiency on multiple subtasks</cite>.
- Reserve OTBKE for targeted practice under constrained workspace; expect comparable surgical-knot time improvements and robust error reduction, with the added benefit of high-fidelity checklist-based mastery. <cite id="803587f7-1">OTBKE reduced surgical-knot time by ~360 s and lowered technical errors</cite>. <cite id="f38b9769-0">Proficiency criteria combining time, OSATS procedural, and knot quality approximate expert performance</cite>.
- Integrate both to enhance learner readiness: evidence supports a sequence—origami box folding first, then outside-the-box knot tying—to comprehensively build and refine laparoscopic psychomotor competence. <cite id="803587f7-1">Both methods are effective; OBFE may precede OTBKE to optimize foundational skills and targeted refinement</cite>.

Title: Comparative Effectiveness of Origami-Box-Folding and Outside-the-Box Knot-Tying Exercises in Laparoscopic Surgical Training: A Prospective Cohort Study
Snippet: Background/Objectives: Minimally invasive surgical techniques require precise psychomotor skills distinct from those used in traditional surgery. Simulation-based training is essential for skill acquisition without patient risk. This study compared two prevalent training methodologies: the Origami-Box-Folding Exercise (OBFE) and Outside-the-Box Knot-Tying Exercise (OBTKE). Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 84 surgical residents (34 OBFE, 50 OBTKE) from General Surgery, Obstetrics–Gynecology, and Urology underwent pre- and post-intervention assessments. Performance metrics included completion times for surgical and square knots, out-of-visual-field instrument instances, needle drops, tissue lesions, and self-assessment via 5-point Likert scales. Behavioral Observation Research Interactive Software quantified performance objectively. Data were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for within-group comparisons and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for between-group differences. Results: Both methodologies significantly improved surgical knot-tying performance. Surgical knot completion time decreased by 316.65 s (OBFE) and 360 s (OBTKE) with no significant between-group difference (p = 0.96). For square knots, OBFE exhibited significantly greater improvement with a 278 s reduction versus 169 s for OBTKE (p = 0.02). Technical errors decreased similarly in both groups. OBFE showed greater improvement in self-rated surgical knot knowledge (p = 0.03) and larger effect sizes for self-assessment measures (0.84–0.87 vs. 0.77–0.85). Conclusions: Both OBFE and OBTKE effectively improve laparoscopic skills in surgical residents. OBFE is particularly beneficial for square knot efficiency and self-rated knowledge enhancement, while OBTKE focuses on targeted knot-tying training. These findings support the implementation of both methodologies in surgical education, potentially in sequence—OBFE for foundational skills and OBTKE for advanced refinement.

Title: The effect of residency training on arthroscopic knot tying and knot stability: which knot is best tied by Orthopaedic surgery residents?
Snippet: Three of the most common arthroscopic knots in the literature were tested in this study: the SMC knot, the Weston knot, and the surgeon's knot (Baumgarten and Wright 2010). The SMC and Weston knot are sliding knots while the surgeon's knot is a static, non-sliding knot. After obtaining Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, these knots were taught to orthopaedic surgery residents at our institution, the trainees, by a fellowship trained sports medicine orthopaedic surgeon, the instructor. Education consisted of each knot being demonstrated by the instructor with an arthroscopic knot simulator followed by a period of hands on practice with the same simulators. The "SAWBONES" (Pacific Research Laboratories) "FAST" (Fundamentals of Arthroscopic Training) box-trainer was utilized by the instructor to demonstrate the various arthroscopic knots. Each knot was demonstrated by the instructor five successive times while verbally explaining how the knot is tied. The trainees were then given up to thirty minutes to practice all three knots on the box-trainer simulator. The instructor was available during the practice period to answer any questions and assist the residents with knot tying. Formal testing did not begin until the resident felt ready to proceed or thirty minutes of practice had elapsed. Trainees were not formally "approved" to proceed by the instructor and only trainees themselves determined when they were appropriate to begin formal testing. Formal testing consisted of 3 SMC knots, 3 Weston knots and 3 surgeon's knots during the initial session. Following a one-week washout period the same 9 knots were again tied at a second session. Therefore, each resident tied a total of n = 18 knots. A single orthopaedic sports medicine fellow tied the same number of knots to serve as a positive control and allow for a baseline comparison for the study cohort. The knots were tied on an arthroscopic knot-tying simulator using standard arthroscopic portals and knot pusher. Upon completion, the knots were carefully slid off of the arthroscopic testing apparatus without violating the integrity of the knot. The knot tails were then cut to a length of 5 cm and placed into de-identified bags to blind the researchers during biomechanical testing.

The adapted OSATS checklist for laparoscopic knot tying evaluates the needle delivery/load, suturing, and knot tying separately. In order to provide the subjects with the most realistic and objective assessment possible, only the Procedural Checklist was used, excluding items that were not assessable on the box trainer in the present setting (maximum achievable score of 13) [2]. 

The checklists were available as online questionnaires and each score was recorded. In addition, the time required for each knot was measured. The time limit per laparoscopic knot was 20 min. The effect of residency training on arthroscopic knot tying and knot stability: which knot is best tied by Orthopaedic surgery residents?
documents.snippet: Three of the most common arthroscopic knots in the literature were tested in this study: the SMC knot, the Weston knot, and the surgeon's knot (Baumgarten and Wright 2010). The SMC and Weston knot are sliding knots while the surgeon's knot is a static, non-sliding knot. After obtaining Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, these knots were taught to orthopaedic surgery residents at our institution, the trainees, by a fellowship trained sports medicine orthopaedic surgeon, the instructor. Education consisted of each knot being demonstrated by the instructor with an arthroscopic knot simulator followed by a period of hands on practice with the same simulators. The "SAWBONES" (Pacific Research Laboratories) "FAST" (Fundamentals of Arthroscopic Training) box-trainer was utilized by the instructor to demonstrate the various arthroscopic knots. Each knot was demonstrated by the instructor five successive times while verbally explaining how the knot is tied. The trainees were then given up to thirty minutes to practice all three knots on the box-trainer simulator. The instructor was available during the practice period to answer any questions and assist the residents with knot tying. Formal testing did not begin until the resident felt ready to proceed or thirty minutes of practice had elapsed. Trainees were not formally "approved" to proceed by the instructor and only trainees themselves determined when they were appropriate to begin formal testing. Formal testing consisted of 3 SMC knots, 3 Weston knots and 3 surgeon's knots during the initial session. Following a one-week washout period the same 9 knots were again tied at a second session. Therefore, each resident tied a total of n = 18 knots. A single orthopaedic sports medicine fellow tied the same number of knots to serve as a positive control and allow for a baseline comparison for the study cohort. The knots were tied on an arthroscopic knot-tying simulator using standard arthroscopic portals and knot pusher. Upon completion, the knots were carefully slid off of the arthroscopic testing apparatus without violating the integrity of the knot. The knot tails were then cut to a length of 5 cm and placed into de-identified bags to blind the researchers during biomechanical testing.

documents.snippet: Background/Objectives: Minimally invasive surgical techniques require precise psychomotor skills distinct from those used in traditional surgery. Simulation-based training is essential for skill acquisition without patient risk. This study compared two prevalent training methodologies: the Origami-Box-Folding Exercise (OBFE) and Outside-the-Box Knot-Tying Exercise (OBTKE). Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 84 surgical residents (34 OBFE, 50 OBTKE) from General Surgery, Obstetrics–Gynecology, and Urology underwent pre- and post-intervention assessments. Performance metrics included completion times for surgical and square knots, out-of-visual-field instrument instances, needle drops, tissue lesions, and self-assessment via 5-point Likert scales. Behavioral Observation Research Interactive Software quantified performance objectively. Data were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for within-group comparisons and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for between-group differences. Results: Both methodologies significantly improved surgical knot-tying performance. Surgical knot completion time decreased by 316.65 s (OBFE) and 360 s (OBTKE) with no significant between-group difference (p = 0.96). For square knots, OBFE exhibited significantly greater improvement with a 278 s reduction versus 169 s for OBTKE (p = 0.02). Technical errors decreased similarly in both groups. OBFE showed greater improvement in self-rated surgical knot knowledge (p = 0.03) and larger effect sizes for self-assessment measures (0.84–0.87 vs. 0.77–0.85). Conclusions: Both OBFE and OBTKE effectively improve laparoscopic skills in surgical residents. OBFE is particularly beneficial for square knot efficiency and self-rated knowledge enhancement, while OBTKE focuses on targeted knot-tying training. These findings support the implementation of both methodologies in surgical education, potentially in sequence—OBFE for foundational skills and OBTKE for advanced refinement.

Snippet: This study is a prospective single-arm cohort study examining the relationship between origami crane training and FLS scores in four Japanese medical students. The study participants were four medical students who had never been trained in surgical techniques for laparoscopic surgery. They were already able to fold the origami crane using their hands. These participants underwent origami crane training five days per week for four weeks. During the period, the students were given the task of making one origami crane per day under a laparoscopic dry box (hereafter referred to as origami crane training). The paper used for the origami crane in this study was white on one side, with various colors on the other side. The dimensions were measured 7.5 Â 7.5 cm. This paper is a standard paper and is not a traditional one. 

The training was directly started using this size of the paper without any other prior training using larger or smaller sizes of the paper. The origami crane training was terminated if the participant could not complete the origami crane in 100 min. The completed origami cranes were mutually evaluated for quality. The perfection of the origami cranes (precision, shape, and lack of scratches) was scored on a 15-point scale, and the experimenters evaluated and scored each other (hereafter referred to as the origami crane score). For the unfinished origami cranes, the score was multiplied by the degree of progress (Figure 1). The FLS performed five tasks, each scored according to the manual [5,6]. The FLS tasks were demonstrated by the supervising physician at the beginning of this study and each participant was referred to the FLS training video. After that, each participant did the origami crane training without the supervising physician. The FLS was performed five times before the start of origami crane training (day 0) and at the beginning of each week (day 5, day 10, day 15, day 20). This study was approved by the Asahikawa Medical University Research Ethics Committee (No. 20181). Written informed consent was obtained from the medical students. The results were presented as the mean AE standard deviation of the participants. All analyses were performed using the R software program (version 3.1.2)

Title: The evaluation of the correlation between origami crane training and Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS)
Snippet: Objective How does making origami cranes under a dry box affect Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) scores in medical students? Design Four medical students from Asahikawa Medical University (tertiary hospital) participated. They made origami cranes under a dry box (origami crane training) five days per week for four weeks. The time required to make each origami crane (origami crane time) and degree of completion were evaluated. FLS scores were measured before training and on days 5, 10, 15, and 20. We examined the relationship between “origami crane training” and FLS scores. Results At the beginning of the experiment, none of the participants could complete the origami crane, but they were able to complete it in 31 ± 7 min on day 20. The Total FLS score was 164 ± 48 before the start of training, and 1107 ± 112 on day 20. The average scores of the students closely approached the Proficiency Level for the FLS tasks of peg transfer, loop ligation and extracorporeal ligation (103→228, 61→137, 0→259). The change over time in the average of the increase in Total FLS Score (difference from the first time and each week’s score) improved significantly in four weeks (P < 0.01). Conclusions Origami crane training improved the medical students' FLS scores. We thought that origami crane training mainly enhanced hand-eye coordination and bi-hand coordination.

Snippet: Objectives: As gynecology surgical cases are declining across the country, residency programs can benefit by training residents with simulation. We evaluate five Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) tasks over 12 months. Materials and Methods: This was a retrospective study of 16 obstetrics and gynecology residents. Residents practiced on a FLS simulation box trainer. They were evaluated on completion time and pass/fail performance for the five tasks of peg transfer, precision cutting, loop ligation, suture with extracorporeal knot, and suture with intracorporeal knot. Resident satisfaction with FLS simulation box training was evaluated. Results: We found improvement of reduced time from baseline to 12 months for the tasks of peg transfer, precision cutting, suture with extracorporeal knot, and suture with intracorporeal knot. No time improvement was noted for loop ligation. We only found increased passing rates for the precision cutting task from baseline to 12 months. Residents agreed that simulation training improves surgical skills, improves patient safety, and improves confidence level in the operating room. Conclusion: We found improvement of decreased time with FLS simulator box training for FLS tasks of peg transfer, precision cutting, suture with extracorporeal knot, and suture with intracorporeal knot. We recommend that routine practice with the FLS simulator box trainer will increase resident confidence level and potentially improve surgical outcomes when in the operating room. We recommend including a dedicated portion of the academic curriculum for simulation training. FLS box training can be an essential tool for residency programs in obstetrics and gynecology.

Snippet: With institutional review board approval, 20 first-and second-year general surgery residents who performed Ͻ10 laparoscopic cases as the primary surgeon were equally randomized (10 residents in each arm) to scheduled training sessions at our surgical simulation laboratory or training in the use of a portable, collapsible Train Anywhere Skill Kit (TASKit) (Ethicon Endo-Surgery Cincinnati, OH, USA) trainer. Before randomization, subjects were all trained on appropriate laparoscopic camera skills, instrument handling, object positioning, dissection, ligation, suturing, and intracorporeal and extracorporeal knot tying throughout this study by an experienced laparoscopic surgeon who is a member of the research team. Training was geared toward the FLS set for the assessment examination. 

All subjects had a group orientation to the surgical simulation laboratory, which was within our hospital center and housed both laparoscopic box trainers and virtualreality trainers, as well as TASKit box trainers. The basic FLS tasks required were as follows: peg transfer, pattern cut, ligating loop, and suturing with intracorporeal and extracorporeal knot tying. Each subject performed a single, supervised practice repetition to orient him or her to the computer simulator and laparoscopic box trainer in the surgical simulation laboratory or to the TASKit trainer, depending on his or her randomization. Subjects were required to perform a minimum of 10 supervised repetitions to ensure that the learning curve for novice surgeons reached a plateau. 13 The residents who were randomized to receive the TASKit trainer were instructed to use this mode of training on a weekly basis at their leisure. All residents had full access to the surgical simulation laboratory, virtual-reality simulator, and laparoscopic box trainers.

Title: Towards a better knot: Using mechanics methods to evaluate three knot-tying techniques in laparo-endoscopic single-site surgery
Snippet: Introduction: Knot tying is difficult but important for laparo-endoscopic single-site surgery (LESS). There are several techniques for LESS knot-tying. The operations were assessed on the basis of the time, average load of the dominant hand. Then, forces caused the knots to rupture were measured using a material testing system and used to compare the knots′s strength. Results: The intracorporeal one-hand knot-tying technique presented significantly better time and average load scores than the extracorporeal knot-tying technique (P < 0.01), and the intracorporeal "side winding" technique was more time and average load consuming in comparison to other techniques during the performance of knot-tying (P < 0.01). Title: Original Training for Laparoscopic Surgery by Making an Origami Paper Crane
Snippet: Introduction: The training box is an effective tool used by surgical trainees. Suturing training is the common method of practicing laparoscopic surgery; however, the cost of needles and threads for long-term practice remains a problem. Methods: LOT was performed using a single 7.5 × 7.5 cm origami paper in the training box of laparoscopic surgery. Consequently, the median PT was significantly shorter in the trained group than in the less-trained group (129.0 (62-287) versus 208.5 (127-343) min; p<0.001).
